tagline.text: A Marian pilgrimage site at the top of 252 steps in Baguio

location.label: Location
location.text: Mirador Hill, Dominican Hill Road, Baguio (entrance from the Kayang Street side)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (Holy Week is extremely crowded)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50~300 (per person, covering transport, candles and snacks; check locally whether a separate entrance fee applies)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Lourdes Grotto on Mirador Hill in western Baguio is a Marian pilgrimage site built by the Jesuits in the early 1900s. A climb of 252 white steps brings you to the statue of Mary, a chapel, and views over Baguio and its cathedral.

Lourdes Grotto is a Catholic pilgrimage site on Dominican Hill Road, Mirador Hill, in western Baguio. Modeled on the apparition site at Lourdes in France, its defining feature is the walk up 252 steps to the top of the hill. It is not far in a straight line from Burnham Park downtown, but being on a hill it leaves the city noise behind, and you find a quiet atmosphere of pine trees, flowers and the statue of Mary. Many travelers come, whether or not they are believers, for the views, the stair climb and the history of the buildings.

Its history goes back to the early 1900s. According to sources, the grotto was built in 1907 near the Mirador Jesuit Villa at the initiative of Fr. José Algué, S.J., then director of the Manila Observatory. The Jesuits quarried limestone from the hill and built it up in stages, and the stone stairway from the grotto down to the foot of the hill was finished about five years later and covered with cement. The statue of Mary now in the grotto is said to be a replica of the original carved in 1913 by the renowned sculptor Isabelo Tampinco; the original is described as kept in the new chapel for preservation. The statue follows the description given by St. Bernadette Soubirous: a white robe, a blue sash, a white veil, a rosary with a gold chain, and yellow roses at the feet. The hill was once bare and treeless, but the Jesuits cultivated steps, pines and flowers, and it became the forest shrine you see today.

This shrine is counted among the most visited pilgrimage sites in northern Luzon. One source lists it with Piat Basilica (Cagayan Valley) and Guibang Shrine (Isabela) as a leading pilgrimage destination of northern Luzon. Sources say the National Museum designated the Mirador Jesuit Villa complex, including the grotto, an Important Cultural Property, but the year differs by source (one gives December 2023), so confirm the exact designation from official sources. It is especially crowded on Sundays and during Holy Week, the week before Easter. The same hill also holds a newer park called the Mirador Heritage and Eco Park, with attractions such as a Japanese-style torii gate, a bamboo grove, a peace memorial and the Jesuit Villa. Entry arrangements and fees for the park and the grotto differ between sources, so confirm them locally.

This guide is for travelers staying in Baguio who want a half day of church touring or a viewpoint walk. With 252 steps, bring suitable shoes, water and some stamina, and there is also a road that vehicles can take up, which visitors with limited mobility can use. Because it is a holy site, mind your clothing and behavior, and take care not to disturb worshippers during Mass or prayer. Park hours are given in some sources as roughly 6:00 to 18:00; if you only plan to climb to the grotto, check the on-site notice at the entrance. Whether there is a separate fee, and whether the stairs and the park share an entrance, may vary over time.

The steps are painted white, and vendors at the start sell rosaries and candles. Pilgrims treat the climb as a sacrifice offered in prayer, and for travelers too, walking up is the heart of the experience.

blocks.title: Statue of Mary and the grotto altar

children.text: In the grotto at the top stands a statue of Mary in a white robe with a blue sash. She looks warmly straight at the viewer. The original from 1913 is said to be preserved in the chapel, with a replica in the grotto.
On the hill there is a chapel where Mass is held, and visitors can light a candle and pray. Mass times change with the season and must be confirmed locally.

blocks.title: Statue of Christ and summit views

children.text: Around the summit there is a sculpture of Christ, and in good weather you can look down on the rooftops of Baguio and the twin spires of Baguio Cathedral.

This building was once a weather observatory and a Jesuit residence and is now used as a retreat house. It stands on the same hill as the grotto and helps you understand the historical context. According to the park's information, the building that was once a telephone station and caretaker's house has become Café Iñigo, which sells cakes and drinks.
A memorial area with a Japanese-style torii gate and a peace bell. The bell is described as made from an unexploded bomb recovered on Mirador Hill after the bombing of Baguio in World War II.

A walking path modeled on the bamboo forest of Kyoto. It is described as having a natural, forest-like feel, and you can see it together with the nearby park area. The park also has a Rock Garden trail of boulders and steps, so sneakers are a good idea.

items.title: Morning pilgrimage route
items.subtitle: Climbing the steps quietly in the early hours

children.text: Take a taxi or jeepney from downtown to the Lourdes Grotto entrance on the Kayang Street side. The sun is not yet high, so it is good for photos and there are few people.
At the foot of the steps, look at the vendors selling candles and rosaries and buy a candle if you need one.
Climb the 252 steps slowly. Rest along the way and enjoy the pines, flowers and the view toward downtown.
At the grotto at the top, pray for a moment or stand quietly and take in the statue of Mary. If you want to light a candle, follow the instructions there.
See the chapel and the statue of Christ, and enjoy the view toward downtown.
Come back down and have breakfast on Kayang Street or downtown.
How long the ascent and descent take depends on your fitness. Some stretches of the stairs are steep, so do not rush.

items.title: Half day on Mirador Hill
items.subtitle: The grotto, the park and the view together

children.text: After lunch, take a taxi to Mirador Hill and climb the grotto steps.
After seeing the summit and the chapel, move to the park area and look at the bamboo grove and the peace memorial.
Near sunset, watch the sun go down from the peace memorial. In clear weather you are said to see the villages to the west and toward Lingayen Gulf.
Come down before dark and return to downtown.
Entrance fees and opening hours for the park area differ between sources. Check official information before you visit.

By car there is a route up along Dominican Hill Road, and a road along the side of the hill is described as letting vehicles reach near the top.
Visitors with limited mobility are known to be able to go up by vehicle.
The road is dark at night, so come down before sunset, and for a taxi, arrange your ride back toward downtown in advance.

Most of the route is steps and outdoor sections, so the weather has a big effect. In the dry season from November to May the sky is clear, views are good and the steps are not slippery. In the rainy season, fog and rain block the view and wet steps are dangerous. In the hours around sunrise and sunset photos turn out well if the sky is clear, but the steps are dark after sunset, so come down promptly.

During Holy Week, the week before Easter, pilgrims crowd in and the steps are packed as if in a queue. If you want to see religious events, that time is meaningful, but if you want to stay quietly, early on a weekday morning is better. One source says it went at sunrise and found no one there, which was good for photos.

There are not many large lodgings near Lourdes Grotto, so most travelers stay downtown around Burnham Park or Session Road and go as a half-day trip. Downtown has a wide choice of hotels, guesthouses and Korean-run guesthouses.

For meals it is best to eat at restaurants below Kayang Street or downtown, and the park area is described as having a cafe selling cakes and drinks. Baguio has many Korean restaurants, so you can eat Korean food downtown when you miss it. Outside food may be restricted, so check in advance.
It is convenient to prepare water and simple snacks before going up the hill. There are not many places to rest around the summit, so please be considerate and take your trash back with you.
Even though vehicles can go up the road beside the steps, walking up is what brings out the meaning of this shrine. If you have time, use the steps.
Early morning or around sunset has fewer people and lower temperatures, making the climb easier.
With 252 steps, bring sneakers and water. It is fine to rest along the way.
If you want to buy and light a candle locally, use the stalls at the foot of the steps.
At the grotto at the top, take care when taking photos not to block the view of people who are praying.
The statue of Mary is of great religious significance, so it is polite to remove your hat and behave quietly.
It is very crowded on Sundays and during Holy Week, so go on a weekday morning if you can.
In the park area pets and outside food are known to be restricted, so check before you visit.
If you have limited mobility, ask on site whether there is a road by which a vehicle can go up.
This is a religious shrine, so avoid very revealing clothing and do not photograph people at prayer without permission.
The steps are steep and long, so people with weak hearts or knees should not overdo it.
Steps and paths are slippery on rainy days, so bring an umbrella and non-slip shoes.
Entrance fees and hours differ between sources, so confirm them locally.
Watch for pickpockets and the like on Sundays and during Holy Week.
Mass times and events change from year to year, so check with the parish if needed.
The city's landmark church, whose two spires can be seen from the top of the grotto. You can add it to your itinerary for a church tour.
A lake park in the heart of downtown, convenient as a starting point for catching a jeepney or taxi.
Baguio's shopping and dining street. After visiting the grotto, it is a good place to come down and rest.
An area of pine forest and former resort grounds, easy to continue to on the same day.
